props.title: Evil Dead II

sections.content: Evil Dead II revolutionized horror-comedy by cranking both scares and slapstick to 11. Sam Raimi's hyperkinetic camera movements and Bruce Campbell's physical comedy created a totally new horror language. Where The Evil Dead (1981) played its cabin-in-the-woods terror straight, the sequel embraced absurdist gore and Three Stooges-style physical humor. That chainsaw-hand sequence? Pure twisted genius. Campbell's Ash Williams fighting his own possessed hand ranks among cinema's greatest comedy sequences, while the practical effects and stop-motion demons still disturb decades later.

sections.content: Evil Dead II's influence exploded across horror. Cabin in the Woods (2011) directly references its tropes. Re-Animator (1985) and Dead Alive (1992) embraced similar gonzo gore-comedy. The film's manic energy and practical effects inspired a generation of horror directors like James Wan and Mike Flanagan. Its DNA lives in everything from Tucker & Dale vs Evil (2010) to Ready or Not (2019).

Raimi's innovative camera techniques - particularly the "demon cam" rushing through the woods - influenced countless horror films. The Evil Dead (2013) remake paid direct homage while amping up the gore. Modern horror-comedies like Drag Me to Hell (2009) and Jennifer's Body (2009) owe their tonal balance to Evil Dead II's perfect blend of screams and laughs. SUBHEAD: The Legacy of Practical Effects

sections.content: Evil Dead II's practical effects by Mark Shostrom stand as a masterclass in pre-CGI horror. The possessed Linda's stop-motion dance, the laughing deer head, and the grotesque neck-stretching demonstrate an artistry largely lost in modern horror. The Thing (1982) and Hellraiser (1987) similarly prioritized practical effects, but Evil Dead II's comedic edge made its gore more palatable while no less impressive.
